content: A group of experts with specialized skills in critically evaluating research evidence, implementing evidence-based recommendations, developing guidelines, and addressing clinical practices, policies, and programs related to maternal and perinatal health, as well as a consumer representative, was assembled. Their expertise spanned various thematic areas within maternal and perinatal health. From this pool, 16 external experts and relevant stakeholders were invited to participate in updating the recommendations. This diverse group included individuals with expertise in research, guideline development, gender equity, clinical practice, policy, and consumer representation, particularly in the prevention and treatment of peripartum infections. The GDG appraised the evidence used to inform the recommendations, provided guidance on interpreting this evidence, and formulated the final recommendations based on drafts prepared by the WHO Steering Group. The group reached unanimous consensus on the recommendations included in the final document. The GDG members are listed in Annex 1. The Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG), convened by WHO, included guideline methodologists and systematic review teams tasked with conducting or updating systematic reviews, appraising evidence, and developing evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks. A systematic review on the effects of vaginal preparation with antiseptic agents for women undergoing cesarean section was updated, with 14 additional trials (involving 4,443 women) included since the last review. This review served as the primary source of evidence for the recommendation. Relevant randomized controlled trials were screened, and data were analyzed using specialized software, such as RevMan and GRADEpro, to critically appraise the evidence. Evidence on values, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility was derived from a mixed-methods systematic review. This review included perspectives from women and healthcare providers on the use of antiseptics to prevent infections during childbirth. Additional studies on the availability and quality of antiseptic agents in lowand middle-income countries were also considered. While no cost-related outcomes were reported in the included trials, expert opinion suggested that implementing this intervention might slightly increase costs in settings where it is not already practiced. However, the low cost of antiseptic agents and minimal resource requirements for implementation could make it cost-effective. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach, which rates evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low based on factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency of results, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Findings from qualitative reviews were appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which evaluates methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance to the review question. The WHO Steering Group supervised the preparation of evidence summaries and EtD frameworks in collaboration with the ESG. These frameworks systematically considered evidence on prioritized interventions across domains such as effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The GDG reviewed these materials and provided feedback before and during the GDG meeting, where they collectively formulated the recommendations. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants, with no opposition expressed. All GDG and ESG members were required to disclose any potential conflicts of interest, which were reviewed and managed according to WHO procedures. Where conflicts were deemed insignificant, experts were required to declare them openly at the beginning of the GDG meeting. The final guideline document was prepared by the WHO Steering Group, reflecting the deliberations and decisions of the GDG. It was reviewed and approved by the GDG and an external review group (ERG) of independent experts. Peer reviewers provided input to address factual errors and improve clarity, which were incorporated into the final document. These principles align with good clinical practices to improve maternal and perinatal health outcomes, including the prevention and treatment of infections during childbirth.
